title: Replacing a Hard Question
paragraphs: In nineteen fifty, the British mathematician Alan Turing published a paper that opened with a deceptively simple question: can machines think? Because the words think and machine are hard to define, he proposed replacing the question with a practical test. He called it the imitation game. He wrote it when electronic computers were still very new.

In the game, an interrogator sits in one room and exchanges written messages with two hidden players. One is a person; the other is a machine. If the interrogator cannot reliably tell them apart, the machine is said to have passed. Notice that the test measures behaviour, not inner experience. The idea is that if conversation alone cannot reveal the difference, then the machine deserves to be taken seriously.

That distinction explains why the test remains controversial. A program might produce convincing replies without understanding anything it says. Even so, the proposal changed the debate, because it replaced an endless argument about definitions with something that could be tried in practice. Later researchers have proposed many variations, but the original setup is still the best known.
